## Model 1 | Design

::: {.eyebrow}
Direct exchange-rate relationship
:::

::: {.formula}
$$
\log REER_{it} = \alpha_i + \beta_1 GPR_{it} + \beta_2 WGI_{i,t-1}
+ \beta_3 (WGI_{i,t-1}\times GPR_{it})
+ \boldsymbol{\gamma}^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{X}_{i,t-1} + \varepsilon_{it}.
$$
:::

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="49%"}
::: {.card}
<div class="card-title">Variables</div>

- $REER$: real effective exchange rate
- $WGI$: one of six governance dimensions
- $GPR$: country GPR, standardized within country
:::
:::
::: {.column width="49%"}
::: {.card}
<div class="card-title">Controls and estimation</div>

- $\mathbf X$: policy rate, inflation, log oil, log VIX, log global EPU, financial development, debt/GDP
- Country fixed effects; country-clustered standard errors
:::
:::
:::

::: {.footnote}
WGI is centered. Its coefficient is evaluated at standardized GPR = 0; the interaction measures how the GPR association changes with WGI.
:::

## Model 1 | Three ideas for interpretation

```{=html}
<div class="idea">
<div class="idea-number">01</div>
<div>
<div class="idea-title">Distinct institutional measures and timing</div>
Voice and accountability reflects participation; government effectiveness, public services; rule of law, legal enforcement; and corruption control, public-sector integrity. These differ from the macro controls, but may still be correlated. Lagging WGI helps with timing; it does not eliminate reverse causality.
</div>
</div>

<div class="idea">
<div class="idea-number">02</div>
<div>
<div class="idea-title">GPR after adding WGI</div>
The GPR coefficient is statistically insignificant in all six WGI specifications, evaluated at average WGI. This does not by itself establish that adding WGI caused the loss of significance.
</div>
</div>

<div class="idea">
<div class="idea-number">03</div>
<div>
<div class="idea-title">Institutions and the exchange-rate level</div>
WGI coefficients are positive in all six specifications and significant in five at 10% (one at 5%). Stronger institutions may support confidence and a stronger REER; currency stability requires a separate volatility test.
</div>
</div>
```

::: {.footnote}
WGI effects are evaluated at average country GPR. Country-clustered inference; these results support interpretation, not a causal conclusion.
:::

## Model 1 | Intuition and qualitative arguments

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="49%"}
::: {.card}
<div class="card-title">Intuition</div>

Institutions may affect the credibility of policy responses when geopolitical uncertainty rises.

<div class="card-title">Alternative interpretation</div>

Institutional scores may proxy for other slowly changing economic features; country fixed effects do not remove time-varying confounding.
:::
:::

## Model 2 | Design

::: {.eyebrow}
Original six-country specification
:::

::: {.formula}
$$
x_{it} = \alpha_i + \pi_1 GPR_{it} + \pi_2 WGI_{i,t-1}
+ \pi_3 (WGI_{i,t-1}\times GPR_{it})
+ \pi_4\log VIX_{t-1} + \pi_5\Delta IP_{i,t-1} + u_{it}.
$$
:::

::: {.formula}
$$
\log REER_{it} = \mu_i + \theta\,\widetilde{\widehat{x}}_{it}
+ \boldsymbol{\delta}^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{X}_{i,t-1} + \eta_{it}.
$$
:::

::: {.small}
- $x$: Hodrick–Prescott log trend of nominal exports; $\Delta IP$: year-over-year industrial-production growth.
- $\widetilde{\widehat{x}}$: first-stage fitted export trend demeaned within country; $\mathbf X$ is the exchange-rate control set from Model 1.
- GPR, WGI, their interaction and IP growth are excluded from the second-stage equation. The staged interpretation depends on exclusion and instrument-strength assumptions.
:::

## Model 2 | Findings and interpretation

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="49%"}
::: {.card}
<div class="card-title">Significant results</div>

- WGI is negative at 5% for VA, RL and CC, evaluated at average country GPR.
- Fitted exports are negatively associated with log REER for VA, RL and CC.
- No WGI × GPR interaction is significant at 5%.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="49%"}
::: {.card}
<div class="card-title">Conclusion</div>

The negative institutional association with exports is contrary to our prediction; it does not establish that weaker institutions cause exports to rise.

<div class="card-title">Possible mechanism</div>

Export booms may coincide with commodity or exchange-rate shocks that are not fully captured. [Review evidence.]
:::
:::
:::

::: {.footnote}
Only six country clusters; the reported partial F is low for GE and RQ. Exclusion restrictions and weak instruments require further scrutiny.
:::

## Model 2 | Intuition and qualitative arguments

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="49%"}
::: {.card}
<div class="card-title">Intuition</div>

Productive capacity and global financial conditions may influence exports, which may then be associated with the exchange rate.

<div class="card-title">Competing explanations</div>

Commodity dependence, reverse causality, or time-varying omitted factors could produce an unexpected sign.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="49%"}
::: {.card .placeholder}
<div class="card-title">Qualitative argument</div>

[Add evidence on export composition and country-specific episodes.]

<div class="card-title">Questions for review</div>

[Assess exclusion restrictions, first-stage relevance and the direction of the REER index.]
:::
:::
:::

## Model 3 | Design

::: {.eyebrow}
Inflation and real exports → nominal exports → exchange rate
:::

::: {.formula .compact-formula}
$$
\begin{aligned}
\pi_{it} &= \alpha_i^{\pi} + a_1 M_{i,t-1} + a_2 r_{i,t-1}
 + a_3GPR_{it} + a_4WGI_{i,t-1} + a_5(WGI_{i,t-1}GPR_{it}) + u_{it}^{\pi},\\
x^R_{it} &= \alpha_i^R + b_1\Delta IP_{i,t-1} + b_2\log VIX_{t-1}
 + b_3GPR_{it} + b_4WGI_{i,t-1} + b_5(WGI_{i,t-1}GPR_{it}) + u_{it}^{R},\\
x^N_{it} &= \alpha_i^N + c_1\widetilde{\widehat{\pi}}_{it}
 + c_2\widetilde{\widehat{x^R}}_{it} + c_3\log VIX_{t-1}
 + c_4\Delta IP_{i,t-1} + u_{it}^{N},\\
\log REER_{it} &= \mu_i + d_1\widetilde{\widehat{x^N}}_{it}
 + \boldsymbol{\delta}^{\mathsf T}\mathbf X_{i,t-1} + \eta_{it}.
\end{aligned}
$$
:::

::: {.footnote}
$M$: import share of GDP; $r$: policy rate; $\pi$: inflation; $x^R$, $x^N$: real- and nominal-export log trends. Tildes denote within-country demeaning of fitted series. $\mathbf X$ is the Model 1 exchange-rate control set, including lagged observed inflation. The stages are fitted sequentially.
:::

## Model 3 | Findings and interpretation

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="49%"}
::: {.card}
<div class="card-title">Significant results</div>

- Fitted real exports are positively associated with nominal exports in five of six columns at 5%.
- Fitted nominal exports are negatively associated with log REER for VA and RL at 5%.
- Fitted inflation is not significant at 10% in the nominal-export equation.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="49%"}
::: {.card}
<div class="card-title">Conclusion</div>

The real-export channel is more consistently visible than the inflation channel in these estimates.

<div class="card-title">Possible mechanism</div>

Greater real export volumes may raise nominal export values; exchange-rate effects may depend on the composition and pricing of exports.
:::
:::
:::

::: {.footnote}
These are associations from sequential fitted regressions, not established causal mediation. Only five country clusters are available.
:::

## Model 3 | Intuition and qualitative arguments

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="49%"}
::: {.card}
<div class="card-title">Intuition</div>

External shocks and institutions may influence prices and production separately before affecting nominal exports and exchange rates.

<div class="card-title">Competing explanations</div>

Import dependence, price pass-through and commodity cycles could alter the apparent export channel.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="49%"}
::: {.card .placeholder}
<div class="card-title">Qualitative argument</div>

[Add supporting evidence or illustrative episodes.]

<div class="card-title">Questions for review</div>

[Review instrument validity, uncertainty through multiple stages and alternative channel explanations.]
:::
:::
:::

## Capital-flow volatility | Design

::: {.eyebrow}
Equation (2) with one WGI dimension
:::

::: {.formula}
$$
vol_{it} = \alpha_i + \beta_1 GPR_{it}^{z} + \beta_2 WGI_{i,t-1}
+ \beta_3 (WGI_{i,t-1}\times GPR_{it}^{z})
+ \boldsymbol{\gamma}^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{X}_{i,t-1} + \varepsilon_{it}.
$$
:::

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="49%"}
::: {.card}
<div class="card-title">Outcome</div>

- $vol$: three-month standard deviation of gross portfolio inflows, billion dollars
- $GPR^{z}$: country article share, standardized within country
- $WGI$: rule of law, government effectiveness, or regulatory quality, lagged and centered
:::
:::
::: {.column width="49%"}
::: {.card}
<div class="card-title">Controls and estimation</div>

- $\mathbf X$: policy rate, log industrial production, inflation, log oil, log VIX, log global EPU, financial development, central-bank independence, debt/GDP
- Country fixed effects; country-clustered standard errors
:::
:::
:::

::: {.footnote}
Table 2's GPR coefficient of 0.867 is a paper reference with no WGI term. Ukraine, Thailand, Indonesia, the Philippines and South Africa have no complete month.
:::

## Subsample design

::: {.eyebrow}
Ten emerging economies
:::

::: {.formula .compact-formula}
$$
\begin{aligned}
y_{i,t}^{j}&=\beta_1 GPR_{i,t}^{z}+\beta_2 WGI_{i,t-1}+\beta_3(WGI_{i,t-1}\times GPR_{i,t}^{z})\\
&+\gamma'X_{i,t-1}+\delta_i+\varepsilon_{i,t}
\end{aligned}
$$
:::

::: {.small}
$y^{j}$: capital-flow volatility or log real exchange rate.
:::

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="49%"}
::: {.card}
<div class="card-title">Top and bottom groups</div>

- **Sample**: 10 emerging economies with complete months
- **Split**: top three and bottom three on each WGI aspect, 2000–2021 average
- **Left out before ranking**: Indonesia, the Philippines, South Africa, Thailand, Ukraine
:::
:::
::: {.column width="49%"}
::: {.card}
<div class="card-title">What is estimated</div>

- **GPR**: standardized within country on the months in that regression
- **WGI**: lagged score, not centered, so GPR is the effect at a score of zero
- **WGI × GPR**: change in the GPR association for a one-point higher score
:::
:::
:::

::: {.footnote}
Two completed checks: rank all ten; then remove China, rank the remaining nine again, and re-estimate the top three and bottom three. Country fixed effects. Controls are lagged one month.
:::

## What stays the same

```{=html}
<div class="idea">
<div class="idea-number">01</div>
<div>
<div class="idea-title">Exchange rate, low-score groups</div>
Mostly not a buffer: voice and accountability, political stability, and government effectiveness stay negative in the bottom three. A higher score goes with a weaker real exchange rate when GPR is higher.
</div>
</div>

<div class="idea">
<div class="idea-number">02</div>
<div>
<div class="idea-title">Two positive exceptions</div>
Rule of law and control of corruption: the bottom-three exchange-rate interactions stay positive after China is removed, 0.031 and 0.039, both significant at the 5 percent level or better. A higher score goes with a stronger real exchange rate when GPR is higher.
</div>
</div>

<div class="idea">
<div class="idea-number">03</div>
<div>
<div class="idea-title">What changes</div>
Government effectiveness: the bottom three become Colombia, Brazil, and Mexico. The exchange-rate interaction is −0.043 and the volatility interaction is −1.545, both significant at the 1 percent level. Regulatory quality in the new bottom three is −0.019, significant at the 10 percent level.
</div>
</div>
```
